captions.instagram:
What is Hooke's law?

Pull twice as hard and a spring stretches twice as far. That one line from 1676 weighs your onions, clicks your pen, carries your car and tunes your guitar. Hang masses on 3D springs, bounce a car over a speed breaker, jump off a bridge on a bungee, and stretch steel until it snaps.

→ Hooke’s law: pull twice as hard and a spring stretches twice as far. F = k × x.
→ Set it bouncing: one swing takes 2π √(m ÷ k), however big the bounce.
→ A spring balance: each kilo stretches the spring the same 1 cm, so the scale is even.
→ A car rides on springs. Without a working damper, a speed breaker sets it bouncing.
→ Bungee: the fall’s energy, m g h, ends up stretched into the cord as ½ k x².

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/hookeclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: What is Hooke's law? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Pull twice as hard and a spring stretches twice as far. That one line from 1676 weighs your onions, clicks your pen, carries your car and tunes your guitar. Hang masses on 3D springs, bounce a car over a speed breaker, jump off a bridge on a bungee, and stretch steel until it snaps.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/hookeclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/hookeclear

In this video:
• Twice the pull, twice the stretch. A spring stretches in proportion to the force on it: F = k × x.
• Springs store energy and keep time. A stretched spring stores ½ k x², the area under the line.
• Weighing and clicking. Because stretch is proportional to load, a spring balance can have evenly spaced marks.
• Riding on springs. A car's corner spring squeezes about 10 cm under its share of the weight and would bounce about 1.5 times a second, so a damper turns the bounce into heat.
• Past the elastic limit. Steel obeys Hooke's law only to about 0.1 % stretch.
